questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a declared column type commits you to
questions.learningObjective: say what a declared column type rules in and rules out
questions.stem: A table declares its column of delivery dates as text because the source system wrote one row as 03/04 and the rest as 2026-03-05. What has the declared type committed the column to?

options.text: The strings will be compared character by character, so the two spellings of a date can sort inconsistently against each other
The values are still dates underneath, so any later sort will place them in true chronological order with no further work
options.misconception: believes a declared text column still sorts by the calendar meaning of its contents

options.text: The malformed row will be reported as an error the moment the column is read, because text is not allowed to hold a date
options.misconception: expects a declared text column to reject a value that merely looks like a date

options.text: Both spellings will be stored as the same instant, because two ways of writing one calendar day mean the same thing to any reader
options.misconception: assumes the reader resolves the ambiguity instead of the column carrying it forward

questions.explanation: A declared type is a promise about how values will be compared, not a claim about what the values mean. Text comparison walks the characters left to right, so 2026-03-05 begins with a digit that outranks the zero in 03/04, and the ambiguous row lands wherever the character order puts it rather than where the calendar puts it. The single sensible fix is to parse the column into a real date type and let the parser reject the row it cannot read, so the problem surfaces as one named row rather than as a silently misordered table. The other three options each assume the tool will rescue the column after the decision has already been made.
questions.hint: Ask how a text column decides which of two values comes first, and whether that rule knows anything about months.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A number written on a label
questions.learningObjective: identify what a mean claims when the column holds labels
questions.stem: A satisfaction survey stores its five response levels as the integers 1 through 5, and a colleague reports the mean response as 3.6. What has that mean quietly claimed?

options.text: That the five levels are equally spaced points on one scale, so a step from 1 to 2 is the same size as one from 3 to 4
That most respondents chose the level nearest 3.6, since a mean of labels always falls beside the commonest label
options.misconception: believes a reported mean reveals the most popular response

options.text: That each person supplied a measured quantity rather than a chosen label, which is what turns a label into a magnitude
options.misconception: reads a label code as though it recorded a measurement of that size

options.text: That the labels may be averaged because they are written as numbers rather than as words, so the notation licenses the operation
options.misconception: believes writing a label as a digit makes the label a quantity

questions.explanation: A mean is only meaningful when the gaps between the values are the same size, and that is exactly what a rating scale asserts: the move from dissatisfied to neutral is meant to be as large as the move from neutral to satisfied. Averaging the codes therefore reports a position on the scale, which is a fair thing to want, but it silently adopts the equal-spacing assumption and reports it in units nobody chose. The subtler damage is to any downstream method: a model handed these codes will happily use the difference between 5 and 4 as evidence, and a tree will happily split between 3 and 4 as though the boundary were a fact about the world rather than a numbering convention.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true about the gaps between 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 before a difference between them means anything.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Three marks of an absent value
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the different claims carried by different missing markers
questions.stem: One column records hours worked and uses an empty string for a shift that was never entered, a null for a shift that was cancelled, and minus one for a shift lost to a broken terminal. What has the column done to its own missing data?

options.text: Made three different claims about absence, so any one fill rule will mean three different things in the three places it is applied
Recorded the same absence three times over, because an empty string, a null and a negative marker all report that nothing is there
options.misconception: believes every missing marker carries an identical claim about what is absent

options.text: Reduced absence to one category, because a value that is not a real number of hours is a value that reports no hours at all
options.misconception: reads any non-numeric marker as a statement that the quantity is zero

options.text: Buried three separate faults in one column, since a reader has no way to tell which of the three markers is the authoritative one
options.misconception: treats several missing markers as an ambiguity of authority rather than as distinct meanings

questions.explanation: Each of the three markers is an assertion about a different world: nothing was keyed in, something was deliberately cancelled, or a record existed and was lost. A fill rule written once and applied to all three therefore asserts something the column never said, and the usual symptom is a plausible-looking column whose zero group is a mixture of never-worked, cancelled and lost shifts. The repair is to read each marker for what it claims before deciding what to do, and that decision differs sharply by kind: a cancellation may be a true zero, a lost record is ignorance and wants a fill, and a never-keyed shift is a question for whoever owns the data.
questions.hint: Ask, for each marker, what a person would have to know for it to be the honest description of that shift.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: When the mean is the right fill
questions.learningObjective: judge when mean imputation is defensible and when it is not
questions.stem: A feature records the length of a support call in minutes, its distribution is close to symmetric, and 4 percent of entries are missing at random. Which single fill is defensible, and what makes it defensible?

options.text: The mean of the entries present, because in a symmetric distribution the centre estimated from the rest estimates it for the gaps too
The median of the entries present, because the median is the only centre that a symmetric distribution is guaranteed to preserve
options.misconception: believes the median is the sole centre statistic valid on symmetric data

options.text: Zero for every gap, because a call with no recorded length is a call that took no time and deserves a zero
options.misconception: reads an unrecorded value as a measured zero

options.text: The value from the previous row, because consecutive calls from the same customer run to similar lengths in this data
options.misconception: assumes neighbouring rows are interchangeable samples of the same thing

questions.explanation: Mean imputation writes an estimate of the centre, and it is defensible exactly when the centre of the recorded values is a fair stand-in for the centre of the missing ones. Symmetry is the condition that buys this, because in a symmetric distribution the mean and the median sit on the same point and a handful of gaps cannot move the estimate far. The interesting failure is not the four percent that is filled, it is the shrinkage: every filled entry sits exactly on the centre, so the column loses a little of its spread, and a downstream model that depends on spread is being handed a slightly tidier world than the one that existed.
questions.hint: Ask which statistic estimates the middle of a roughly symmetric cloud, and what happens to the spread when every gap lands on it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: When the median is the right fill
questions.learningObjective: choose the median over the mean for a column with distant extremes
questions.stem: A feature records annual household income in dollars, one entry is one billion, and the remaining entries all sit between twelve thousand and ninety thousand. Which single fill is defensible here?

options.text: The median of the entries present, because one value that far out drags the mean toward itself and leaves the median where the mass is
The mean of the entries present, because averaging the recorded entries is the standard way to estimate a missing one
options.misconception: treats averaging as the default estimator regardless of the column's shape

options.text: The trimmed mean of the entries present, because setting one value aside changes the centre of a distribution that is not symmetric
options.misconception: believes a trimmed mean corrects a distribution it has not shown to be lopsided

options.text: The mode of the entries present, because the commonest income is the safest stand-in for a household of any kind at all
options.misconception: believes the most common value represents an unseen member of the same population

questions.explanation: The median summarises where the middle of the ordered column sits, and no single value, however absurd, can move it, which is precisely the property that matters when one entry may be real but unrepresentative. The mean has no such protection: one entry at a billion among ordinary incomes is enough to drag the mean up by tens of millions, and a fill written at that level would be an invented household unlike any in the table. The honest caveat is that the median hides a real spread rather than correcting it, so a decision that depends on the width of the income distribution still has to look at the whole column and not at the filled value.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two centres a single enormous value can move, and how far.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mode imputation on a category
questions.learningObjective: say what mode imputation buys and what it invents
questions.stem: A column records which of three shift patterns a worker was on, and 12 of its 240 entries are blank. What does filling every blank with the modal pattern achieve, and what does it cost?

options.text: It keeps the column usable as a category, and it invents 12 assignments that no record in the table actually supports
It keeps the column usable as a category, and it costs nothing because the modal pattern was already the commonest
options.misconception: believes filling with the commonest value leaves the column's distribution unchanged

options.text: It turns a categorical column into a numeric one, and it gives each blank a length of zero rather than a name
options.misconception: thinks a mode fill assigns a quantity rather than a category

options.text: It should be replaced by declaring a fourth pattern, because a blank is genuinely a pattern of its own
options.misconception: treats an unrecorded value as a recorded category rather than as an absence

questions.explanation: On a column with no arithmetic to do, the mode is the only centre available, and filling with it is the standard move; the cost is not the arithmetic but the claim. Twelve workers are recorded as having worked the pattern that most workers worked, and nothing in the table says any of them did. That matters most when the filled category is later used as a group, because a 12-row phantom group looks exactly like a real one until someone asks how those shifts were actually assigned. Keeping the blanks as their own category is usually the more honest choice, provided the method being used can be told that a category means unrecorded.
questions.hint: Ask how many of those 12 workers have any record saying which pattern they worked.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: When dropping beats filling
questions.learningObjective: argue for dropping rows from a scatter of random missingness
questions.stem: Two percent of a 40,000-row table are missing the value of the column the model most depends on, and those rows are scattered evenly across every other column rather than clustered anywhere. What argues for dropping them instead of filling them?

options.text: The gaps are scattered rather than clustered, so dropping removes a small random slice and leaves the surviving rows representative of the whole
Two percent is above the one percent figure often quoted as acceptable, so any missingness at all is already too much to fill
options.misconception: treats a share of missingness as unacceptable regardless of how it is distributed

options.text: Filling would mean inventing 800 values, and a table containing invented values is no longer a record of anything observed
options.misconception: believes any imputation at all makes a dataset cease to be observational

options.text: The gaps fall on the column the model depends on, so the surviving rows are too few to support a reliable fit
options.misconception: assumes missingness in a key column leaves too little data rather than less complete data

questions.explanation: The argument for dropping is about what the missingness is attached to, not about how much of it there is. When the gaps are scattered with respect to everything else in the table, the rows that survive are a simple random sample of the original and every summary of them stays unbiased, which is the condition that lets a later conclusion generalise. When the gaps cluster, dropping is a decision about a subpopulation and the survivors are no longer representative, and that is the case where filling or a stated exclusion is the more honest move. The 39,200 remaining rows are ample for almost any purpose, so the arithmetic is never what the argument is really about.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rows you would keep still look like the rows you dropped.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A duplicate row and a duplicate key
questions.learningObjective: separate a repeated key from a repeated row
questions.stem: An orders table holds one row per order line, 48 rows repeat an order identifier, 18 of those are exact copies of another row, and the remaining 30 are genuine second lines on the same order. What does deduplicating on the identifier alone do?

options.text: Deletes 30 real order lines along with the 18 copies, because a repeated key is being read as though it proved a repeated row
Deletes only the 18 exact copies, because two rows that agree on the key are the same row however many other columns disagree
options.misconception: assumes a shared key settles identity regardless of the other columns

options.text: Deletes 48 rows of which 18 were duplicates anyway, so the real data lost is less than the row count suggests
options.misconception: credits the deletion of real rows against the deletion of copies

options.text: Deletes nothing at all, because a repeated key only counts as a problem when every column repeats along with it
options.misconception: believes key collisions are harmless without checking what the other columns hold

questions.explanation: A duplicate row is a record that says the same thing twice, and a duplicate key is only the possibility that two records might do so; at a grain of one row per order line, two lines on one order are two different events and the key is supposed to repeat. Deduplicating on the key therefore enforces a uniqueness constraint the data never promised, and the damage is silent because the surviving table still looks well formed: one row per order, no repeats, and 30 real purchases quietly gone. The correct test is whether the whole row repeats, and where a real feed has no natural row identity, that question has to be settled with the system that produced the table.
questions.hint: Ask what the table promised about its key, and whether two lines on one order are the same event.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: An outlier and a valid extreme
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a valid extreme from a faulty record
questions.stem: A courier's recorded delivery times are 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9 hours on five ordinary days and 96 hours on a sixth day when the depot was closed all afternoon. Which statement about that 96 is right?

options.text: It is a valid extreme, because a real closure produced it, and the response is to model the closure rather than delete the day
It is an outlier by definition, because it lies more than three standard deviations above the mean of the other five days
options.misconception: treats a distance from the mean as proof that a record is wrong

options.text: It must be removed first, because a value like that drags the mean far above the typical delivery and misleads any average
options.misconception: removes a real event purely because it moves a summary statistic

options.text: It is almost certainly a keying error, because no courier can take four days to deliver inside the same city boundary
options.misconception: judges a value impossible without reference to any record of what happened

questions.explanation: A rule of thumb about standard deviations is a way of finding values worth looking at, not a verdict on them, and the verdict comes from the world rather than from the arithmetic. Here something real happened: the depot closed, so a four-day delivery is an accurate record of a bad day and deleting it removes a genuine hazard from the picture the business is trying to see. The productive move is to give the closure its own column, so that the delivery time can be modelled conditionally, and a model that has seen such days before can then distinguish a stuck parcel from a closed depot instead of treating both as noise.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything in the world happened to produce the extreme, and who knows.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why distance-based methods need a common scale
questions.learningObjective: explain what standardising changes for a distance-based method
questions.stem: Two features describe the same activity in different units, one running from 0 to 1 and the other from 0 to 10000, and a method that compares cases by distance is about to use both. What does standardising them change?

options.text: The relative weight the two features carry in every distance, because comparable spreads stop one feature dominating each comparison
Nothing about the distances, because a rescaling of this kind leaves every comparison between two cases unchanged
options.misconception: believes rescaling inputs cannot change which case is nearest to which

options.text: The number of features the method ends up using, because a rescaled column is treated as independent of the others by it
options.misconception: believes rescaling a column removes its correlation with the other columns

options.text: The target the method is fitted against, because standardising is applied to the answer rather than to the inputs it is given
options.misconception: believes the rescaling step is applied to the outcome column

questions.explanation: A distance is a sum of squared differences, so a feature measured in thousands contributes a term thousands of times larger than one measured in fractions, and the method then effectively ignores the smaller-scale feature altogether. Standardising divides each column by its own spread, which sets every contribution to the same footing and makes the resulting distances mean something about disagreement across the features rather than about their units. What it does not do is make the two features independent, or stop them being redundant, so standardising a redundant pair leaves the method double-counting the same information even though the arithmetic is now fair between columns.
questions.hint: Ask how big a squared difference from the large-scale column is next to one from the small-scale column.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why gradient methods need a common scale
questions.learningObjective: explain what standardising changes for a gradient-based fit
questions.stem: A model is fitted by gradient descent, one input column holds values in the millions and another holds values between 0 and 1. Why does putting both on a comparable scale help that fit converge?

options.text: The two columns then move the prediction by comparable amounts per step, so no single gradient is dominated by the large-scale column
The gradient of each column then has the same sign, so the search stops zig-zagging back and forth between the two of them
options.misconception: confuses scale imbalance with a sign disagreement between gradients

options.text: The surface of the loss then becomes flat, so the fit no longer needs a step size and can run straight to the optimum
options.misconception: believes rescaling the inputs removes the need to choose a step size

options.text: The two columns then carry the same information, so halving one and doubling the other leaves the fitted answer alone
options.misconception: believes rescaling makes two columns interchangeable in every respect

questions.explanation: A single step size has to serve every coefficient at once, and the gradient of a coefficient is proportional to the spread of the column it multiplies, so a column in the millions produces a gradient thousands of times larger than one bounded by 1. At a step size big enough to move the first, the second is flung far past its own optimum and has to be walked back, which is the long narrow valley that makes these fits crawl. Standardising shortens the valley into something closer to a bowl, and the shape rather than the arithmetic is what a step size is really coping with.
questions.hint: Ask how far each column's coefficient can move under one shared step size.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The ordinal imputation trap
questions.learningObjective: identify the value mean imputation writes onto an ordinal scale
questions.stem: A five-point rating column has 12 percent of its entries missing, and the team fills each gap with the mean of the entries present, which is 3.8. What is actually wrong with what has been written in?

options.text: The scale has no 3.8, so the fill invents a value the instrument cannot express and quietly shrinks the spread of responses
Nothing at all, because 3.8 falls between 3 and 4 and any respondent choosing either would have produced a value very close
options.misconception: accepts an unattainable value because it lies between two attainable ones

options.text: The mean is simply the wrong centre here, and the median of 4 would be right because it is a value the scale allows
options.misconception: locates the fault in the choice of statistic and not in the scale

options.text: The scale itself is fine but its spread is not, so the fill should be the standard deviation of the recorded responses
options.misconception: believes a spread statistic can be substituted for a level on a rating scale

questions.explanation: A five-point instrument produces five values and no others, so writing 3.8 adds a sixth thing to the column that no respondent could ever have produced, and the entry then looks like data to every stage downstream. The quieter harm is to the spread: 12 percent of the column pinned exactly on a point between 3 and 4 pulls the variance down and narrows what the distribution appears to be, which flatters any summary and flatters any method that measures how unusual a case is. Choosing the median instead fixes the attainability problem but leaves the shrinkage, and the honest treatment for an unrecorded rating is usually a category of its own.
questions.hint: Ask how many different answers a five-point question can produce, and where 3.8 sits among them.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Counting cells after a clean
questions.learningObjective: compute the cell count left after dropping columns and duplicate rows
questions.stem: A table holds 250,000 rows and 14 columns. A team drops 3 columns and then removes 1,180 rows that are exact copies of other rows. How many cells remain in the table?
questions.explanation: Removing the duplicate rows first leaves 250,000 − 1,180 = 248,820 rows, and the column count falls from 14 to 14 − 3 = 11, so the table holds 248,820 × 11 = 2,737,020 cells. The other route gives the same figure: the full table holds 250,000 × 11 = 2,750,000 cells, and the 1,180 deleted rows account for 1,180 × 11 = 12,980 of them, leaving 2,750,000 − 12,980 = 2,737,020. The two orders agree because a cell count is a product, and getting the same answer either way is a cheap check that the column drop was not applied to the row figure.
questions.hint: Take the surviving rows first, then multiply by the number of columns you kept, and check by subtracting the deleted rows' cells from the full table.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The mean of a rating column
questions.learningObjective: compute a weighted mean over a small set of rating levels
questions.stem: A five-point rating column holds 400 responses, of which 80 chose 1, 160 chose 3 and 160 chose 5. What is the mean of the column?
questions.explanation: Weighting each level by how often it was chosen gives 80 × 1 + 160 × 3 + 160 × 5 = 80 + 480 + 800 = 1,360, and 1,360 ÷ 400 = 3.4. Expressed as shares instead, the column is 20 percent at 1, 40 percent at 3 and 40 percent at 5, so 0.2 × 1 + 0.4 × 3 + 0.4 × 5 = 0.2 + 1.2 + 2.0 = 3.4, the same figure by a different route. The number is arithmetically exact and evidentially weak, because it describes where the responses sit on a scale nobody measured and it hides that nobody chose 2 or 4 at all.
questions.hint: Multiply each level by the number of times it was chosen, add, then divide by the total number of responses.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A blank that means zero
questions.learningObjective: count the rows a sentinel reading of missing data swallows
questions.stem: A column of 500 rows records hours booked, and its data dictionary says a blank means zero. Twelve rows are blank and 80 rows carry an explicit zero. How many rows hold a zero under that reading of the column?
questions.explanation: The blanks and the explicit zeros join into one group, so 120 + 80 = 200 rows carry a zero. The check from the other side is that 500 − 200 = 300 rows hold a genuine positive number of hours, and 300 + 200 returns the full 500. The reason this is worth counting rather than assuming is that the two sources mean different things and the dictionary has collapsed them: a blank may be an unentered shift, a cancelled shift or a lost record, and reading all of them as zero converts an admission of ignorance into a statement that nothing happened.

questions.topic: Turning a missing percentage into a count
questions.learningObjective: convert a reported missing rate into a number of rows
questions.stem: A column of 46,000 rows is reported as 3.5 percent missing. How many rows is that, to the nearest whole row?
questions.explanation: Three and a half percent of 46,000 is 46,000 × 3.5 ÷ 100 = 1,610 rows. The independent route is to take one percent first: 46,000 ÷ 100 = 460 rows per percent, and 460 × 3.5 = 1,610. Both give a whole number, which is worth confirming because a rate quoted to one decimal place usually conceals a fraction of a row, and a team that fills a fraction of a row by rounding has quietly changed the size of the table. questions.topic: The value mean imputation writes
questions.learningObjective: compute the value a mean fill writes into a single gap
questions.stem: A column of delivery times is missing exactly one entry, and the five recorded times are 4, 8, 10, 12 and 16 minutes. What value does mean imputation write into the gap?

The symmetry argument reaches the same number without any arithmetic: 4 and 16 sit six either side of 10 and 8 and 12 sit two either side, so the entries balance around 10 and a balanced set has its mean on the centre. questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How far the median fill sits below the mean
questions.learningObjective: compute the gap between the mean and the median of a skewed column
questions.stem: One entry of a column is missing and the five recorded values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 20. The team fills the gap with the median rather than the mean. By how much does the value written in sit below the mean?
questions.explanation: The values sum to 2 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 20 = 36, so the mean is 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2, and sorted the middle of five is 4, so the fill sits 7.2 − 4 = 3.2 below the mean. Clearing the fraction first confirms it: (36 − 20) ÷ 5 = 16 ÷ 5 = 3.2. The single 20 is the whole story, since it lifts the mean without shifting the median at all, and a fill placed 3.2 units below the centre is a materially different guess from one placed on the centre, which is why the choice between the two statistics is a real decision rather than a preference.

questions.topic: The share a mode fill creates
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of a categorical column after a mode fill
questions.stem: A shift column reads A, B, B, C, blank and blank. The team fills both blanks with the modal pattern. What share of the finished column is the modal pattern?
questions.explanation: Filling both blanks with B gives A, B, B, C, B, B, so B appears four times in six rows, which is 4 ÷ 6 = 0.6667. The independent route is to count the additions rather than to recount the column: B was already there twice, both blanks become B, and the row total is unchanged at six, so the count rises from 2 to 2 + 2 = 4 over the same 6. The denominator is the trap. Three in four would be the share among the four rows that actually carried a pattern, and quoting that figure would quietly shrink the group of unknowns to nothing before the fill happened.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The cost of a blanket drop
questions.learningObjective: count the usable rows lost by dropping every row with any gap
questions.stem: A table holds 800 rows. Sixty of them are missing a value for a feature, and 45 of those same 60 also lack the value the model must predict. Dropping every row with a missing feature discards all 60. How many rows with a perfectly usable target does that destroy unnecessarily?
questions.explanation: Of the 60 dropped rows, 45 had no target to contribute anyway, so the genuinely wasted rows are 60 − 45 = 15. The same 15 comes from counting what survives the alternative: filling the feature would have kept 800 − 45 = 755 usable rows, and dropping keeps 800 − 60 = 740, a difference of 755 − 740 = 15. The decision therefore costs 15 cases out of 740, not 60, and 60 is the figure a reader is shown if nobody separates the rows that were unusable anyway from the rows a fill could have rescued.
questions.hint: Subtract the rows that were already worthless from the rows the drop removed, and check against the difference in usable totals.

questions.topic: What a key dedupe really removes
questions.learningObjective: count the real records a key-based dedupe destroys

The independent route counts what should have survived: the table holds 1,200 lines of which 18 are redundant, so 1,200 − 18 = 1,182 distinct lines exist, and the dedupe keeps 1,200 − 48 = 1,152, leaving 1,182 − 1,152 = 30 destroyed. questions.hint: Count the copies as harmless and the second lines as losses, then check by comparing the rows that should have survived with the rows that did.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How far one extreme moves a mean
questions.learningObjective: compute the change in a mean caused by one added extreme
questions.stem: Five recorded delivery times are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 9 hours. A sixth day is then added at 300 hours after a depot was closed all afternoon. By how many hours does the mean of the column rise?

Adding the sixth day gives 24 + 300 = 324 over 6 rows, which is 54 hours, and the mean has risen by 54 − 4.8 = 49.2. The independent route uses the property that adding one value moves the mean by the gap between that value and the old mean, divided by the new count: (300 − 4.8) ÷ 6 = 295.2 ÷ 6 = 49.2. A single genuine closure has therefore moved the typical delivery from under five hours to fifty-four.
questions.hint: Compute the old mean, the new mean, and subtract; then confirm with the gap rule for adding one value.

Dividing 3,150 by the original 30 would give 105 and would charge the trimmed values to the ones that stayed.
questions.hint: Remove the trimmed hours from the total, count the values that remain, then divide one by the other.

The independent route runs the arithmetic backwards: a standardised value of 3 means three spreads, three spreads of 5 is 15, and 15 above the mean of 50 is 65. The figure is the reason a standardised column is readable at a glance, though what it cannot say is whether three spreads is remarkable in this business, which is a judgement about the column and not about the arithmetic.

questions.stem: A model is fitted by gradient descent, one input column carries values around 100 and another around 0.1, and the search moves every coefficient by 0.01 on each step. By what factor does the first column's contribution to the change in the prediction exceed the second's?

The independent route cancels the shared step entirely and compares the two input magnitudes: 100 ÷ 0.1 = 1,000, which is the same factor and is the more useful way to see it, because the step size is common to both columns and so cannot be what creates the imbalance. Any step size big enough to move the first column meaningfully throws the second far past its own optimum, which is the long thin valley that makes such fits crawl.

The independent route is to take the remaining fifth directly: 2,000 ÷ 5 = 400, and holding back one fifth is the same statement said the other way round. The size of the block is unremarkable and its timing is everything, because a holdout earns that name only while nothing has read it. The first comparison that scores those 400 rows converts them into training data, and from then on the figure is a description of those 400 rows rather than an estimate of performance on the next 400.

The independent route takes a fifth of the positives directly: 200 ÷ 5 = 40. The independent route is to count the folds that train rather than the one that tests: nine tenths of 5,000 is 0.9 × 5,000 = 4,500. Every row is therefore trained on nine times and tested on exactly once, which is what makes the average of the ten scores a steadier estimate than any single split, since the result no longer depends on which tenth happened to be held out. questions.topic: What a log does to a range
questions.learningObjective: compute how far a log transform compresses an additive range
questions.stem: A right-skewed feature runs from 4 up to 4,096, and on a base-2 logarithmic scale the same two values sit at 2 and 12. The log has turned an additive range of 4,092 into a range of 10. By what factor does it shorten the range?
questions.explanation: The additive range is 4,096 − 4 = 4,092 and the logarithmic range is 12 − 2 = 10, so the range is shortened by a factor of 4,092 ÷ 10 = 409.2. The independent route counts the compressions directly: 4,096 ÷ 4 = 1,024 and 1,024 = 2^10, so the two values are exactly ten doublings apart, which is precisely the length of the log scale, 12 − 2 = 10. The factor is that same comparison read the other way. What the transform buys is not a smaller column but a scale on which equal steps mean equal ratios, so a value ten times another looks the same wherever in the range the pair sits.
questions.hint: Divide the original range by the range after the transform, and confirm by counting how many doublings separate the two extremes.

questions.stem: A target column holds the values 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000. Its arithmetic mean is 2,222.2 and its geometric mean is 100. By what factor does the arithmetic mean exceed the geometric mean?

The independent route locates the geometric mean without any root: it is the middle of the ordered column, which is 100, and 2,222.2 is 22.2222 times that middle value. The size of the ratio is the signature of a right-skewed target, because the arithmetic mean is set by the largest few entries while the geometric mean is set by the shape of the whole column, which is exactly why a straight-line fit chases the 10,000 and a fit on a log scale does not.

The column is within specification, since RETURNED is only a different word for RECEIVED in this system's own vocabulary
options.misconception: assumes a new value is a synonym rather than a distinct state

options.misconception: believes the fix for undocumented values is a change of storage type

questions.explanation: A data dictionary is a claim about what a system records, and a claim that has quietly stopped being true is more dangerous than a missing one, because a missing claim is noticed while a false one is trusted. questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a duplicate audit
questions.learningObjective: separate removable duplicates from legitimate repeated keys
questions.stem: A duplicate audit covers 1,200 rows and finds 48 that repeat an order identifier. Comparing whole rows, 18 of those 48 are exact copies of another row and the other 30 differ in at least one column. What should the audit conclude?

options.text: There are 18 duplicated rows to remove, and the remaining 30 are legitimate repeats of a key the table's own grain allows
There are 48 duplicates to remove, because a repeated order identifier is on its own proof of a duplicated row
options.misconception: treats a repeated key as sufficient evidence that the row is a copy

options.text: There are 30 duplicates to remove, because a row differing from another in any column must be a keying mistake
options.misconception: assumes any disagreement between two rows signals a data-entry error

options.text: There is nothing to remove, because two rows that disagree on a column are by definition two separate real events
options.misconception: concludes that disagreement between rows settles the question in one direction

questions.explanation: A duplicate row is a record that says the same thing twice, and the only reliable test is whether every column repeats, which here identifies 18 of the 48. The other 30 repeat a key while differing somewhere, and at a grain of one row per order line two lines on the same order are two different purchases that the key is supposed to group. The disagreement is evidence of distinctness rather than of error, since a genuine second line will differ in the item, the quantity or the price. The count that matters for a report is therefore 18, and a script that dedupes on the key will quietly remove 30 real purchases while looking as though it had merely tidied up.
questions.hint: Ask which rows repeat every column, and what the table promised about repeating a key.

questions.learningObjective: pair a holdout with a plan for when it is read
questions.stem: A team must fit a model and then report an honest estimate of how it will perform on cases it has never seen. Which pairing of the two actions produces an estimate that means what it says?

options.text: Set a holdout aside first and read it exactly once at the end, after every modelling choice has been made
Fit on all the rows first and split afterwards, since a model fitted on more rows is more accurate than one fitted on fewer
options.misconception: values fitting-row count above the honesty of the resulting estimate

options.text: Set a holdout aside first and use it to choose between candidates, since comparing models on it is the fairest way to compare them
options.misconception: believes a block used to choose a model is still an untouched block afterwards

options.text: Fit on everything and report the fitted score, since the fitted score is the least biased estimate available for that model
options.misconception: takes the score on the cases a model was fitted to as an out-of-sample estimate

questions.explanation: The value of a holdout is entirely a matter of when it is read, because every read is a decision made using those rows and every decision made using them makes the final figure a description of them rather than an estimate of anything else. Setting it aside and reading it once at the end means the only thing that shaped the model was the training side, which is the condition under which the score is a forecast. The other three fail in different ways: fitting on everything first makes any later split cosmetic, comparing candidates on the holdout turns it into a validation set, and the fitted score measures how well a model memorised what it was shown, which is a number every model can be flattered by.

questions.topic: Finding the cause of a row-count surprise
questions.learningObjective: choose the check that identifies a duplicated dimension key
questions.stem: A reporting query joins 5,000 order rows to a customer table and the result comes back with 5,340 rows. Before any of the totals are trusted, which check should be run?

options.text: Count how many rows each customer identifier has in the customer table, then repair that table if any repeats
Recount the order rows before the join, since a changed count must have come from the table being joined from
options.misconception: assumes the order table is the only possible source of extra rows

options.text: Sort the joined result by order identifier and drop repeats, since a clean report never shows an identifier twice
options.misconception: believes removing repeated keys from the output is an adequate repair

options.text: Recalculate every total using a distinct count, since distinct counting always repairs an inflated join
options.misconception: believes a different aggregation conceals rather than fixes row multiplication

questions.explanation: A join can only return more rows than its left input when some left row matched more than one right row, and the only place that can be decided is the right-hand table, so checking key uniqueness there is the first move rather than the last. The other three all act downstream: recounting the order table cannot find a fault it does not contain, dropping repeated identifiers from the output destroys exactly the second lines the table was built to hold, and switching totals to a distinct count leaves the inflated rows sitting in the table for the next query to find. The 340 excess rows here trace to 12 duplicated customer records, which is a fact about the customer table and not about the query.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the join could offer one left row a second match, and check that side for repeated keys.

questions.topic: Missingness that is not random
questions.learningObjective: choose a handling for missingness that clusters on a variable
questions.stem: A column of 50,000 rows is 4 percent missing, and those gaps cluster heavily among customers in the smallest billing band. Which handling of the gaps is defensible?

options.text: Report the missingness by band and analyse within band, because clustered gaps mean the recorded rows are not a random sample
Fill every gap with the overall mean, since a column's mean is the best available estimate of any one missing value
options.misconception: believes a single average is a fair stand-in regardless of where the gaps sit

options.text: Fill every gap with the modal recorded value, since the commonest value is the safest guess for an unrecorded one
options.misconception: assumes the commonest recorded value is also commonest among the unrecorded cases

options.text: Drop every row that has a gap, because 4 percent of 50,000 rows is far too few for their loss to matter
options.misconception: judges a drop by how few rows it removes rather than by which rows it removes

questions.explanation: Missingness that clusters on a variable is carrying information, and discarding that information is what the choice has to protect against. If the smallest band is missing values for a reason specific to that band, then filling with an overall mean imports the other bands' typical behaviour into the one band where it is least true, and dropping the rows removes a segment of the customer base from the analysis entirely. Working within band, or modelling whether a value is missing, keeps the structure visible. The arithmetic size of the gap is the least important of the four considerations here, because 4 percent concentrated in one band can matter more than 20 percent spread evenly.
questions.hint: Ask which rows are missing, not how many, and what the pattern of their absence is attached to.

questions.stem: A pipeline will use both a nearest-neighbour step and a gradient-descent fit, and one input column is recorded in milliseconds while another is a five-point rating. Which preparation is right?

options.text: Standardise both from statistics computed on the training rows only, then carry those same statistics into serving unchanged
Standardise both from statistics computed over the whole table, so the training and serving scales match by construction
options.misconception: believes matching the scales matters more than keeping the serving figures independent

options.text: Standardise the milliseconds column only, since a five-point rating is already on a small and bounded scale
options.misconception: assumes a bounded range means a comparable spread in the distance being computed

options.text: Leave both columns alone, since rescaling is a cosmetic step that alters no distance and no gradient
options.misconception: believes a change of units cannot change the arithmetic of a comparison

Fitting the scaling on training rows and saving those numbers is what makes serving honest, since a new case is then measured against the same yardstick the model was fitted with rather than against one that has moved to meet it. The other two failures are the ordinary ones: leaving a bounded rating unscaled because its range is small ignores that a small range and a small spread are different things, and skipping scaling altogether lets the milliseconds column decide every distance and every gradient.
questions.hint: Ask where the centre and spread used for the transform came from, and whether the held-out rows helped choose them.

questions.topic: Encoding a categorical column
questions.learningObjective: choose an encoding that does not invent distances between categories
questions.stem: A model must use a column of eleven delivery regions and a column of customer tenure in months. Which encoding hands the model something usable without inventing structure?

options.text: One indicator column per region and tenure left as a number, since a region has no distance between regions and a tenure does
One column numbering the regions alphabetically from 1 to 11 and tenure as a number, since both are then columns of numbers
options.misconception: believes numbering a category makes the numbering carry no implied order

options.text: One indicator column per region and one per distinct tenure value, since every distinct value of any column deserves its own column
options.misconception: applies the same treatment to an ordered quantity as to an unordered category

options.text: One column holding the region names and tenure replaced by its mean, since a model can read a name but cannot read a spread
options.misconception: assumes a method cannot use a numeric column directly

Numbering the regions alphabetically is the classic trap, because it asserts that the region numbered 1 sits one step from the region numbered 2 and nine steps from the region numbered 10, an ordering produced by the alphabet. Tenure is the opposite case: it is a quantity where 3 months really is less than 30, so the original number already means what the model needs and needs no expansion.

questions.topic: A feature that only exists after the answer
questions.learningObjective: choose a feature that is available at the moment of prediction

options.text: Contacts opened in the last 30 days and already closed when the prediction is made, so the input exists at that moment
All contacts opened in the last 30 days, since a customer who will churn opens more of them than one who will not
options.misconception: assumes a strong correlation survives the removal of information unavailable in time

options.text: Contacts closed in the last 30 days, since a closed case is one the customer cared enough to see through
options.misconception: believes a narrow window on a late-arriving count is free of leakage

options.text: The lifetime total of contacts, since a running total is always available and can never leak
options.misconception: takes availability at prediction time as proof that a feature cannot leak

Restricting to contacts already closed is honest and costs some signal, since the newest and most telling contacts are excluded, but what survives is a number the model could actually have had. The alternative that looks safest is the lifetime total, and it fails for the same reason in a subtler form: it is a total that keeps accumulating, so a model fitted on completed periods learns a relationship between a final total and an outcome that will not hold for a customer part-way through one.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why an out-of-date dictionary is worse than none
questions.learningObjective: explain the failure mode of documentation that has stopped being true
questions.stem: Explain why a data dictionary that has quietly stopped matching the system is more dangerous than a table with no dictionary at all, and say what a cheap check against it would catch.

answer.exemplar: A missing dictionary announces itself, so a reader knows to go and ask what a column means, while an out-of-date one is trusted and answers a question nobody asked. Every downstream decision is then made correctly according to a false description, which is why the errors are not confined to the column concerned: a status that has quietly acquired a fourth state changes what the target means, a date that changed format changes what the rows describe, and a count whose definition shifted changes every rate built on it. The cheap check is to enumerate the distinct values each categorical column actually holds and set them beside the list the dictionary allows, reporting the difference by both distinct value and row count, since a column can be almost entirely within its documented range and still hold a handful of values nobody described. Ask the system owners what each unexpected value means and when it first appeared, because a value that began on a particular date means the column holds two definitions and any model trained across that date has been fitting both at once.

questions.explanation: The danger of stale documentation is that it transfers authority without transferring accuracy: a reader who finds no dictionary spends effort finding out, and a reader who finds a wrong one does not. A wrong definition of a feature is worse than no definition because it survives review, because a colleague checking the work will check it against the same document, and because the people best placed to notice are usually the ones no longer working on the system. The audit that catches it is unglamorous and cheap, being a distinct-value listing per categorical column compared against the allowed set, and the two numbers worth reporting are how many unexpected values exist and how many rows carry them, since those count different risks.
questions.hint: Consider who reads a missing document differently from a wrong one, and what a distinct-value listing would show.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What deduping on a key destroys
questions.learningObjective: explain why a key-based dedupe removes real records
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a duplicate row and a duplicate key, and say why deduplicating on the key silently removes real records even when the table still looks well formed afterwards.

answer.exemplar: A duplicate row is a record that says the same thing twice, which can be established by comparing every column. A duplicate key is only the possibility that two records might, and at a grain of one row per order line a key is supposed to repeat, because one order has several lines. Deduplicating on the key therefore enforces a uniqueness constraint the data never promised, and the result still passes every obvious check: one row per identifier, no repeats, a plausible count. That is what makes the damage silent, since nothing in the shape of the output reports the loss, and the records that disappear are real purchases. The safe test is whether the whole row repeats; where a feed provides no row identifier, the question has to be settled with the system that produced the table rather than by a script, and the count of rows removed by key alone should be reported next to the count of exact copies so that the difference is visible.

questions.explanation: The grain of a table is the agreement about what one row is, and a key is only a label for that agreement. When a table is built at one row per order line, the key identifies the order and the line is identified by the pair, so a repeated key is the expected condition rather than a fault. A dedupe that keeps one row per key is silently converting the table to one row per order, which is a different table with different totals, and the fact that it looks tidy afterwards is the trap rather than the reassurance. Distinguishing the two cases needs a whole-row comparison, and reporting the two counts separately is what makes the decision auditable.
questions.hint: Ask what one row in the table is a record of, and whether the key is meant to be unique in that table.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why imputation shrinks a column
questions.learningObjective: explain the hidden cost that every mean fill adds to a column
questions.stem: Explain why filling missing values with the mean leaves a column that is partly real and partly invented, and say what that does to the column's spread.

answer.exemplar: A mean fill writes the same number into every gap, so after the fill some rows are observations and some are the column's own centre repeated, and nothing in the column distinguishes them. The effect on spread is always downward: a column with real variation in it is being given extra rows with no variation at all, which pulls the variance towards zero in proportion to how much was filled. With four percent filled the change is small and rarely matters, and with forty percent filled the column is substantially tidier than the world it claims to describe. Two further consequences follow. Any summary that depends on how unusual a case is will treat the filled rows as unremarkable by construction, and any model asked to predict spread or to find outliers will be working partly on the filler rather than on the data. Reporting the filled share alongside every summary of the column, and comparing the spread before and after, is the minimum needed to keep the invention visible.

questions.explanation: Imputation is an assertion that the gap held the centre, repeated once per gap, and the cost of that assertion is not confined to the gaps themselves. Adding rows that all sit on the mean reduces the average squared distance from the mean, so the variance falls, and a variance that has been reduced by the fill will be under-reported in every model and every threshold derived from it. The filled rows also share a property no real row has, namely that they are exactly typical, so a method looking for unusual cases cannot see them as unusual however unusual they genuinely were. The honest practice is to keep the count of filled rows next to the column and to say which statistic was used, because the choice between centre and median changes the shrinkage and the attainability question changes the validity.
questions.hint: Ask what the filled rows have in common with each other, and what that does to any measure of how spread out the column is.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a stratified split buys and costs
questions.learningObjective: state the benefit and the limitation of stratifying a split
questions.stem: Explain what a stratified split buys, what it costs, and why a figure computed on a stratified block should not be quoted without saying that it was stratified.

answer.exemplar: A stratified split holds the class share constant across the training and test sides, so a rare class is represented in the test block in roughly the proportion the table holds. What it buys is stability: a block of 200 rows drawn at random might hold 15 or 25 rare cases, and every rate computed on it then swings for reasons that have nothing to do with the model, so the comparison between two candidates becomes a comparison between two lucky draws. What it costs is representativeness, because a block assembled to hold a fixed class share is no longer a random sample of the traffic, and so its figures describe a deliberately balanced case mix rather than the one the model will meet. That is why such a score should be quoted with the word stratified attached: the number is honest about the model and silent about the mix. A team that wants a forecast of production behaviour needs an unstratified holdout or a reweighting of the stratified figures back to the real class shares, which is a separate and non-trivial step.

questions.explanation: Stratification trades one kind of honesty for another. It makes the test block a controlled comparison, in which the only thing that varies between candidate models is the model, and it does so by giving up the property that the block resembles a random draw from the traffic. Both properties are wanted and they cannot both be had from one block, which is why the practice is to stratify for choosing between models and to keep an unstratified holdout for reporting an expected production figure. The silent failure is a stratified score quoted as though it were a production forecast, in which case a rare class is over-represented in the block and the model looks better on it than it will be.
questions.hint: Ask whether the block is still a random sample of the traffic after its class shares have been fixed.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a whole-dataset feature leaks
questions.learningObjective: explain leakage caused by computing a feature across all rows
questions.stem: Explain why a feature computed over the whole dataset leaks even when the rows it was computed from are held back, and say where inside a pipeline the computation has to move.

answer.exemplar: The held-out rows are held out from fitting, not from every earlier step, and a feature averaged across the whole dataset has already absorbed the outcomes of those rows. The model is therefore being handed, as an input, a summary that contains the answer it is being scored against, and it will learn to lean on that summary heavily, which flatters the held-out score by an amount that is invisible and disappears in production. The rule is that every quantity derived from data must be derived inside the fitted part of the pipeline: a mean, a count, a rate, a scaling centre and spread, an encoding fitted on the categories seen, a target average used for ranking. Each of these has to be computed on training rows, stored, and then applied unchanged to held-out and to live rows, so that a live case is measured against the same yardstick rather than one that has moved to meet it. The tell is a score that collapses on data collected fresh at the real prediction moment, and the prevention is to ask of each feature when its value reached its final form.

questions.explanation: Leakage is a timing problem rather than a modelling one, and it survives every check that looks only at the code rather than at the clock. A held-out block is excluded from the fit, so anything computed before the split still contains it, and the fit then discovers a relationship between a summary of the answers and the answers themselves. The mechanism is worth stating precisely: the feature does not predict the outcome, it contains it, so the learned weight on it is large and the held-out score is high for a reason that will not recur. Every derived quantity has the same problem, which is why the fix is structural, namely fitting each transformation on the training side and carrying it forward unchanged, rather than a matter of removing one suspicious column.
questions.hint: Ask when each derived number reached its final value, and whether the held-out rows contributed to it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a log transform does and does not fix
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of a log transform on ratios and on skew
questions.stem: Explain what a log transform does to a skewed feature, why it is a sensible thing to try on a right-skewed target before fitting a straight line, and what it does not repair.

answer.exemplar: A log changes what a step means. On the original scale a step is an addition, so moving from 10 to 100 covers far more of the column than moving from 1,000 to 1,090, and a method that adds up contributions is dominated by the top of the range. On the log scale a step is a multiplication, so the same step means the same ratio everywhere, and a value ten times another looks identical whether it sits at the bottom or the top. That is why a log is worth trying on a right-skewed target before a straight-line fit: the line is then free to describe a roughly constant relationship in ratios instead of being dragged towards the few very large values, and the residual spread usually narrows with it. What the transform does not repair is a genuine relationship change, a value recorded wrongly, or skew that runs the other way, since a left-skewed column is made worse rather than better. Fit the transform on training rows, carry it into serving, and remember that the predictions come back on the log scale and must be returned to the original one before anyone reads them.

questions.explanation: The log earns its place by making the geometry of the column match the geometry of the relationship being modelled. A straight-line fit measures error additively, so on a right-skewed column it spends its effort on the largest rows, and the fit that minimises total squared error is one that predicts those few well at the expense of everything else. Logging replaces addition with multiplication, the top of the column comes down towards the middle, and the fit is then able to spend its effort across the whole range. The limitation is that the transform is a change of scale and not a repair: it cannot fix a value that was recorded wrongly, cannot undo a genuine change in slope, and applied to a left-skewed column it makes the imbalance worse.
questions.hint: Ask what one unit of movement means on each scale, and what the fit is being asked to keep small.

Parsing comes second because the type decides what a missing value looks like and whether two spellings of the same thing can be told apart, so cleaning before parsing means cleaning against the wrong rules. Rebuilding with training-only steps third turns a suspicion into a measurement, because a genuine feature should cost little and a leaking one should cost most of the gap. questions.topic: Working out what a broken column is saying
questions.learningObjective: order the steps that classify a column's non-values before repairing it
questions.stem: A column behaves strangely: some of its entries are blank, some hold minus one, and some hold a value the dictionary never mentions. Put these four steps in the order that leads to a defensible repair.

options.text: Establish what the column is meant to hold and how its values are currently stored in the file
Count the entries that fall outside that meaning, separately for each form the absence takes
Decide, for each form separately, whether the row is unknown, genuinely zero, or a real value
Fill, drop or recode on the strength of those decisions, and record which was applied where

questions.explanation: A repair is only defensible if it is made per form rather than per column, and the order is what makes per-form decisions possible. Meaning comes first, because whether a blank means nothing happened or nobody recorded it depends entirely on what the column is for. Counting comes second and is done separately for each form, since a column whose absences arrive in three different guises has three different problems and one total conceals all three. Deciding comes third, and it is the only genuinely hard step, because the answer differs by form: a cancellation may be a true zero, a lost record is ignorance, and a value the dictionary never mentions needs a conversation with the system owner.
